overview: This bill makes a wide set of changes to how the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the federal agency that regulates the stock market and investment firms, writes rules and operates. Before issuing a rule, the SEC would have to define the problem, weigh costs and benefits through its chief economist, consider the combined effect with other rules, issue the rule only if benefits justify costs, and later check whether major rules worked. Public comment periods would last at least 60 days (30 for imminent harm to investors), the SEC chair would testify to Congress every six months, and the Government Accountability Office would audit the SEC's technology and cybersecurity and periodically review its major rules. It would also eliminate the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, the separate body that oversees auditors of public companies, after two years and move its work into a new office inside the SEC, and it would count repeated violations from the same cause or misstatement as a single violation when setting penalties. The House Financial Services Committee approved an amended version, and it was placed on the House calendar on September 3, 2026.
for: Supporters say the bill makes the SEC show its rules are worth their costs, gives the public more time to weigh in, and folds a costly separate audit regulator into the agency that already oversees it.
against: Critics say the new analysis and comment requirements would slow or block investor protections, and treating related acts as a single violation could sharply reduce penalties for serious misconduct.
